delete.description: Only its owner deletes it: a developer of it gets `owner_only`, and a member `member_only`. Its address, every share of it and its name go at once, so a deploy by that name makes a new app, with an empty disk. The operation succeeds once its host has stopped it and every gateway has dropped its address and shares and closed what was open to it. There's no trash and nothing restores it. While a deploy of it is under way, it's `app_busy`. Once it's deleted, sending it again answers `no_such_app`.

It writes each file at `/app/<path>` on the app's disk, replacing what's there and touching nothing else, runs the app's build there, and then starts the app on what its disk holds, even if the build failed. Without `owner`, a deploy makes your app if you have none by its name; with it, the app must be one you're a developer of.

put.description: The app gets it as an environment variable of the same name. The name is an uppercase letter, then uppercase letters, digits and underscores, at most 64 characters. It can't be one the platform sets, HOME, PATH or PORT, or start with ANYWHERE_, which the platform keeps for its own. The value is UTF-8 text of 1 to 32768 bytes, without NUL characters, kept exactly as sent, in a request of at most 65536 bytes. An app has at most 100 secrets, of at most 1048576 bytes together, names and values. A running app restarts with its new secrets, and the operation succeeds once it has started again, as a deploy's does; an app that isn't running gets them when it next starts. An app you don't have is `no_such_app`, unless the request sets `create_app`, which makes only an app of your own, never with `owner`. A change to a web app that has no address yet succeeds with a warning that says how to give it one. Sending the same request again is safe, and restarts a running app once more.

put.description: The share names their verified email. A member uses it in their browser or with their agent token, as you do, and finds it in `GET /v1/shared-apps`. A developer can also deploy to it, run commands in it, read its logs and set its secrets, naming it with `owner`; only you share it. The app is told their username in the `Anywhere-User` header, and their role in `Anywhere-Role`, where you get `owner`. Someone with no account yet gets the app once they sign up with that email, and can be made a developer only once they have (`developer_needs_account`). Without `role`, a new share is a member's and an existing one keeps its role; another role changes it. An operation that makes someone a developer warns that developers read the app's secrets and that removing one doesn't undo what they changed. The operation succeeds once every gateway admits them as their role says, and, for a change to member, has closed what needed a developer. Sending it again is safe. The email goes in the body, never the path, so no request log holds it.

post.description: device code and no other credential. Until a person approves it, it's `login_pending`, and asking again after `interval_seconds` is safe. The first answer after approval issues a 30-day agent token for the person who approved it, labelled with the machine's name, and ends the login, so no second answer gets a token: `cli_login_used`, even when the first answer was lost, so a request that may have reached the control plane isn't sent again. A login past its 10 minutes is `cli_login_expired`, and an unknown device code `unknown_cli_login`; for each, run `anywhere login` again.
